I have been contacted by a couple of (nice) people in leading roles in other cryptos' foundations. And the question is usually: why #Doge, and why not our coin, that we think is more technically sound?

I usually answer: because #Dogecoin has a dog in it; your coin does not.

I know many who bought #Dogecoin at the peak in January 2018 (around 0.02 USD). Within a few months the price collapsed to 1/10th the value.

Those people had to wait until 2021 to sell at a profit.

But be careful: even this consideration is not a guarantee of anything.

And this is why we keep repeating: buy small amounts at a time; do not play with leverage, ever; do not bet house money, farm money, student loans, or family savings.

Put into crypto only money you can afford to lose or to have locked into an asset long term. #dogecoin

@italia_dogecoin Also remember: in a permissionless project, anybody can do whatever - so if @Tesla tomorrow wants to send 2 engineers to work directly on Dogecoin Core, they can. 

But the Github system of reviewing PRs and core maintainers would keep any excessive influence in check.

@italia_dogecoin Finally, I have faith that the current consensus mechanism (including Github based development, miners' interests, node operators' interests, users' interests) would mitigate excessive influence coming only from one-direction. One needs to trust the process.

@italia_dogecoin I had long discussions about this last year on reddit with Pat Lodder and others and I understand your concerns, which are also shared by other developers.

I personally see this kind of stuff as "added" possibilities, opening more doors instead of closing them. (4/n)

@italia_dogecoin Also, while there are people that can afford to work on Doge for free, many people cannot. Money flowing in can potentially balance out some of these risks as it allows people that could otherwise not have a chance to work on Doge to join development. (3/n)

@italia_dogecoin There is too much money in this industry to prevent moneyed actors (could be miners, exchanges, companies) paying people with influence in the community behind the scenes.

With the structure of the foundation, with good communication, influences can come into the open. (2/n)
@italia_dogecoin It is unavoidable - but I think the same influence seeps into also an open source project that seems, on the surface, not to have "big donors". (1/n)
@italia_dogecoin *to happen, sorry

@italia_dogecoin Tthere are "donors" that bring with them a lot of troubles. To me, they those that play a part in the consensus mechanism Doge is using; so for example, I would not like mining pools paying our developers (as it is happening with the Litecoin Foundation).

@italia_dogecoin Another note. Keep in mind that the Dogecoin Foundation does NOT coincide with #Dogecoin - it is a parallel organization. Anybody can create another foundation with a different purpose and aim.

The ecosystem will be made of many parties contributing to it.

@italia_dogecoin Being pragmatic: I do not think that people's tipping would realistically ever be enough to keep up with the expenses (the legal expenses alone cost a fortune) or with hiring even one or two full time developers for a prolonged period of time.

@italia_dogecoin I see the point (shared by others) but I generally do not agree with this. I think the Foundation's purpose is also to put these donations out there in the open and create a structure to allow them to happens, so the community knows about them. Openness is crucial, though.
